howToReadPaper.title: How to convert a newspaper into GS notes
steps: Read The Hindu / Indian Express editorials for the argument, not the anecdote.
Map every story to a syllabus heading (Polity, Economy, IR, Environment, Science, Bihar).
Write 4–5 lines: what happened, why it matters, constitutional/legal hook, way forward.
PIB is for schemes, indices and official data — copy facts, skip PR language.
Revise weekly: 10 issues, 2 maps, 1 ethics case from real news.

subjects.title: History
subjects.papers: Prelims GS · Mains GS-I · BPSC GS-I
subjects.overview: History in UPSC and BPSC is not a list of kings. It is how power, economy, culture and protest changed over time. Prelims tests facts that sit on a storyline. Mains wants causes, consequences and continuity. BPSC adds Magadha, 1857 in Bihar, Champaran and the JP movement. Read NCERT as the spine, Spectrum for modern India, and keep a one-page Bihar timeline.

modules.title: Ancient India
explain: Start with the Harappan world: planned cities, drainage, craft specialisation, long-distance trade (Mesopotamia), and a script we still cannot read. Decline is a package of climate, river shift and political fragmentation — not a single invasion story. Link this to geography: Indus, Ghaggar-Hakra, monsoon reliability.

The Vedic–later Vedic transition is about pastoral to agrarian life, varna, janapadas and the rise of mahajanapadas. Magadha (Rajgir, then Pataliputra) wins because of iron, forests, the Ganga–Son corridor and ambitious dynasties (Haryanka, Shishunaga, Nanda). This is a BPSC favourite.

Mauryas built the first pan-Indian state we can describe in some detail: standing army, spies, land revenue, Ashoka’s dhamma after Kalinga, and edicts as public communication. Collapse opens space for Shungas, Satavahanas, Kushanas and Sangam south. Guptas are the ‘classical’ template: land grants, Sanskrit culture, Aryabhata, and a looser feudalising polity. Buddhism and Jainism need councils, patrons, cave and stupa architecture, and Bihar sites — Bodh Gaya, Nalanda, Vaishali, Vikramshila.
points: Harappan urbanism, craft, trade, script, decline — always pair with rivers and climate.
Mahajanapadas; why Magadha (iron, Ganga, geography, politics).
Mauryan state, Ashoka’s dhamma, economy, Mauryan art (Sarnath, Dhauli).
Gupta polity, land grants, science, post-Gupta regional kingdoms.

modules.title: Medieval India
explain: Treat the Delhi Sultanate as an administrative experiment: iqta, cavalry, urban markets (Alauddin Khalji), and Indo-Islamic architecture (Qutb, Tughlaq, Lodi). Do not reduce it to battles. Ask what happened to peasants, towns and religion on the ground.

The south and Deccan are equal GS: Vijayanagara’s nayaka system and temple-urbanism; Bahmani successor states; Bhakti and Sufi as social languages that cut across courts. Kabir, Nanak, Chaitanya, the Nayanars–Alvars, and the Chishti silsila are more useful than memorising every raid.

Mughals: mansab, jagir, zabt, sulh-i-kul, painting and architecture. The jagir crisis and later fragmentation matter more than a morality play about Aurangzeb. Sher Shah (Sasaram) is a Bihar-centred case: roads, rupee, sarkar–pargana — a ready-made Mains example of state capacity. Patna Kalam later shows cultural continuity in the region.
points: Sultanate: iqta, market control, architecture, urban economy.
Vijayanagara, Bahmani, Bhakti and Sufi — culture as politics.
Mughal administration, zabt, jagir crisis, art.
Sher Shah in Bihar–Bengal as a governance case study.

modules.title: Modern India & National Movement
explain: Modern India begins with how the Company became a state: Plassey–Buxar, Diwani, Subsidiary Alliance, Doctrine of Lapse. Economy is half the paper: drain of wealth, deindustrialisation, land systems (Permanent, Ryotwari, Mahalwari), famines, railways as both modernisation and extraction. This overlaps GS-III.

1857 is a layered event — army, taluqdars, peasants, religion, communication. For BPSC, zoom to Arrah, Jagdispur and Kunwar Singh. After 1857, Crown rule, associations, Congress, Moderates vs Extremists, Swadeshi, Home Rule.

Gandhian mass politics: Champaran (indigo, 1917 — first satyagraha in India), Kheda, Ahmedabad, Non-Cooperation, Civil Disobedience, Quit India. In Bihar, note peasant movements and 1942. Also keep revolutionaries, workers, women, depressed classes, and the communal question. End with Partition, integration of states, and the Constituent Assembly — the bridge into Polity.
points: Colonisation and economic drain; land revenue systems.
Champaran, NCM, CDM, Quit India; social groups in the movement.

modules.title: Art, culture and ideas
explain: Treat culture as society made visible. Stupa and cave, Nagara–Dravida–Vesara temples, Indo-Islamic arches and gardens, colonial civic architecture. Sculpture from Mauryan polish to Chola bronze; painting from Ajanta to Mughal miniatures and Company/Patna Kalam.

Ideas: Sramana traditions, Bhakti–Sufi vernaculars, reform in the 19th century (Brahmo, Arya, Aligarh, women’s education), print and public sphere. Prelims asks a diagnostic feature; Mains asks patronage, region and social message.
Bihar culture file: Bodh Gaya–Nalanda–Vikramshila, Madhubani, Sonepur, Magahi–Maithili–Bhojpuri literary worlds. Use them as examples, not as a tourist brochure.

modules.title: World history (UPSC GS-I slice)
explain: Industrial Revolution and its social costs; American, French, Russian revolutions as political templates; colonialism and decolonisation; World Wars and the UN; Cold War bipolarity and NAM’s room to manoeuvre.
Keep each event to cause → course in two lines → consequence for Asia/India. This is a short paper slice, not a second optional.

subjects.title: Geography
subjects.papers: Prelims GS · Mains GS-I · BPSC GS-II
subjects.overview: Geography is the map underneath almost every GS paper: climate for agriculture, rivers for disasters, location for industry, migration for Bihar’s economy. Draw while you read. Prelims loves definitions and India maps. Mains wants process + impact + policy. Keep an atlas open next to NCERT and G.C. Leong.
sources: IMD, Survey of India, Bihar Economic Survey maps

modules.title: Physical geography
explain: Geomorphology: Earth’s interior, plate tectonics (divergence, convergence, transform), earthquakes, volcanoes, and landforms of wind, water, glacier and wave. Prelims asks the ‘why’ of a landform (ox-bow, fjord, barchan). Mains asks hazards and human settlement.

Climatology: composition of atmosphere, heat budget, pressure belts, jet streams, monsoon as seasonal reversal plus ITCZ, western disturbances, cyclones (eye, eyewall, energy from warm seas), ENSO as a modulator not the monsoon itself. Practise diagrams of the Indian monsoon onset and retreat.

Oceanography (currents, upwelling, resources) and biogeography (biomes, soils of India — alluvial, black, red, laterite, arid). Soils connect to cropping patterns and to Bihar’s alluvial fertility plus waterlogging.
points: Tectonics, earthquakes, volcanoes, fluvial and glacial landforms.
Monsoon mechanism, cyclones, ENSO, jet streams.

modules.title: Indian geography
explain: Six physiographic units: Himalayas, Northern Plains, Peninsular Plateau, Indian Desert, Coastal Plains, Islands. Himalaya vs peninsula is the master contrast: young fold mountains vs old plateau, snow-fed vs rain-fed rivers, seismic north vs relatively stable south (with exceptions).

Drainage: Himalayan rivers (antecedent, large sediment, changing courses) vs peninsular (graded, east-flowing deltas). Ganga–Brahmaputra–Meghna and the Kosi–Gandak–Son system are exam gold. Resources: coal, iron, petroleum, rare earths — location + environmental cost. Agriculture regions (rice, wheat, cotton, sugarcane, millets) follow climate and irrigation.

Human geography: density, census themes, urbanisation, smart cities, industrial corridors (DMIC etc.), ports. For Bihar, out-migration to Punjab, Delhi, Mumbai and the Gulf is a human-geography + economy + society question.

modules.title: Bihar geography
explain: North Bihar is a floodplain of Himalayan rivers: shifting courses, high water tables, and the Kosi’s avulsion history. South of the Ganga you meet older alluvium and, further south, the fringe of Chhotanagpur — harder rock, minerals next door in Jharkhand, different drought–flood mix.

Floods are not only ‘too much rain’. They are sediment, embankments that trap water, drainage congestion, and climate extremes. Pair this with GS-III disaster management: early warning, reservoirs, non-structural measures, and why embankment-only policy fails.

Agriculture: maize, litchi, makhana, winter vegetables, jute pockets. Agro-climatic zones differ east–west. Irrigation from canals and tubewells; arsenic in some groundwater pockets is a health-geography issue. Industry is thin relative to people — hence migration — but locational logic (Gaya, Muzaffarpur, Begusarai, food parks) still matters.
points: North plains vs southern plateau fringe.
Minerals in neighbouring Jharkhand; industrial map of Bihar.

modules.title: World geography & maps
explain: Places that still appear in Prelims: major currents, deserts, rift valleys, temperate grasslands, important straits and canals, rainforests vs taiga. Pair each with a resource or climate process.
Geopolitical geography: chokepoints (Malacca, Hormuz, Suez, Bab-el-Mandeb), Arctic routes, Indo-Pacific framing. This is IR sitting on a map.
Practise locating India’s neighbours’ capitals and Himalayan passes; BPSC still rewards the eastern Himalaya–Tarai–delta continuum.

subjects.title: Polity & Governance
subjects.papers: Prelims GS · Mains GS-II · BPSC GS-II
subjects.overview: Polity is the rule-book of the Republic plus how it actually runs. Laxmikanth is the index, the Constitution is the text, newspapers are the case file. Every current story about Governors, bills, courts or elections should land on an Article, a body, or a doctrine.

modules.title: Constitutional structure
explain: Preamble (justice, liberty, equality, fraternity; socialist, secular, democratic, republic) is a key to interpretation. Features: length, borrowed provisions, federal with unitary bias, parliamentary executive, independent judiciary, fundamental rights. Amendment (Art. 368) vs basic structure (Kesavananda Bharati, 1973) is the central doctrine question.

Fundamental Rights (12–35), DPSPs (36–51), Duties (51A): harmony and conflict (Champakam, Minerva Mills). Union and State executives, Parliament and legislatures, money bills, ordinance, anti-defection. Judiciary: independence, judicial review, PIL, collegium debates, tribunals.

Federalism: Seventh Schedule, Finance Commission, GST Council, emergencies (352, 356, 360), the Governor as a flashpoint in current affairs. Representation of the People Act and the Election Commission complete the electoral skeleton.
points: FRs, DPSPs, Duties — conflict and harmony.

modules.title: Governance
explain: Sort bodies: constitutional (EC, CAG, UPSC, FC), statutory (NHRC, CIC, Lokpal), executive/regulatory (SEBI, RBI, CCI). Know appointment, removal, and one function each.

Local government: 73rd and 74th Amendments, three-tier panchayats, 11th/12th Schedules, State Election Commission, State Finance Commission. Bihar’s PRIs, reservations, and scheme delivery at the last mile are BPSC-relevant.

Transparency and integrity: RTI, CVC, CAG audit, Lokpal, citizen charters, e-governance, DBT. Social justice: NCSC, NCST, NCBC, women and child commissions, welfare architecture. Governance answers should name a principle, an institution, and a reform — not slogans.
points: Constitutional vs statutory vs regulatory bodies.
Social justice commissions and welfare delivery.

modules.title: Rights, cases and comparison
explain: A short case list is enough if each case teaches a doctrine: Kesavananda (basic structure), Minerva Mills (harmony), Maneka (due process flavour), Bommai (federalism/356), Vishaka (guidelines), Puttaswamy (privacy), Shayara Bano/triple talaq as legislative follow-through, NJAC as appointment politics.
Comparison: parliamentary vs presidential, FPTP vs PR, Indian secularism vs strict separation. Use comparison to sharpen, not to write political science optional answers.
Current affairs should land on one of these doctrines within 24 hours of reading the paper.

subjects.title: Economy
subjects.papers: Prelims GS · Mains GS-III · BPSC GS-II
subjects.overview: Economy is concepts + this year’s Survey and Budget. If you cannot explain inflation, deficit, repo and GST in plain Hindi/English, facts will not save you. Then add Bihar: agriculture, migration, low industrial base, and schemes after 2005.

modules.title: Core concepts
explain: National income (GDP, GVA, real vs nominal), inflation (CPI vs WPI, food vs core), unemployment types. Monetary policy: RBI, MPC, repo, SDF, CRR, SLR, transmission. Fiscal policy: Budget, revenue vs capital, fiscal/revenue/primary deficits, FRBM. Never confuse monetary (RBI) with fiscal (government).

Banking and NBFCs, NPAs, inclusion (PMJDY, UPI), insurance and pensions. GST as a destination-based dual indirect tax; compensation debates are federalism. Finance Commission (vertical and horizontal devolution) is GS-II/III overlap.

External sector: CAD, capital flows, forex reserves, rupee, WTO (agriculture, subsidies, public stockholding), FTAs. Prelims loves definitions; Mains wants trade-offs (growth vs inflation, welfare vs deficit).
points: GDP, inflation, unemployment; repo vs Budget.

modules.title: Development & Bihar economy
explain: Development is not GDP alone: poverty lines, inequality, HDI, SDGs, health and education outcomes, jobs. Agriculture: MSP, APMC, MSP–inflation tension, food security (NFSA), climate risk. Bihar’s maize, litchi, makhana and vegetable belts are concrete examples.

Industry and labour: why Bihar’s factory share is low, power and land, food processing, and the role of remittances from migrants. Infrastructure (roads after 2005, electricity, digital) changed the growth story but the social sector still decides Mains marks.
Read the Bihar Economic Survey for two numbers you can quote: GSDP growth, sectoral shares, unemployment or migration. Pair with national Survey so you can compare.

modules.title: External sector, WTO and industry
explain: BoP: current vs capital, CAD, services surplus, remittances, forex. Rupee as outcome of inflation differentials, flows and risk. Do not confuse FDI (lasting stake) with FPI (portfolio).
WTO: MFN, national treatment, agriculture boxes, public stockholding, fisheries, TRIPS and public health. FTAs are political economy — rules of origin, sensitive lists, services mobility.
Industry: PLI, logistics (Gati Shakti flavour), MSME credit, labour codes as GS-III. Bihar’s industrial thinness is a location and power-and-land story, not a slogan.

subjects.title: Science & Technology
subjects.papers: Prelims GS · Mains GS-III · BPSC GS-II
subjects.overview: Prelims wants Class 6–10 science done cleanly. Mains wants what a technology does to the economy, security, health and fairness. File every ISRO, vaccine or AI headline as application + regulation + equity.

modules.title: Everyday & applied science
explain: Physics: motion, light, electricity, semiconductors at a conceptual level. Chemistry: acids–bases, carbon compounds, polymers, everyday chemicals. Biology: cell, genetics at a light level, human physiology, diseases, nutrition. This block wins easy prelims marks if you revise NCERT, not random PDFs.

Health: vaccines (antigen, memory), antibiotics vs AMR, vector-borne disease in Bihar (kala-azar, encephalitis belts). Energy: solar, nuclear, green hydrogen, storage. Semiconductors and the India incentive story sit at GS-III industry + S&T.
Space: PSLV vs GSLV, navigation (NavIC), Earth observation for farming and floods — a direct bridge to Bihar disaster management. Don’t collect mission nicknames without a use-case.
points: Vaccines, AMR, public health in the eastern plains.

modules.title: Frontier tech (Mains)
explain: AI, platforms and data: productivity vs bias vs labour. Data protection law, CERT-In, critical information infrastructure — this is internal security as much as S&T.

Biotech: GM crops, genome editing (CRISPR), ethics of consent and biodiversity (Cartagena). IPR, patents vs access to medicines. India Stack (Aadhaar, UPI, DEPA) as digital public infrastructure — inclusion and surveillance in the same paragraph.
Write S&T answers in three beats: what it is, where India stands, what governance must do.

modules.title: Nuclear, defence tech and health R&D
explain: Civil nuclear: three-stage programme idea, liability, waste, IAEA safeguards flavour. Defence: missiles as deterrence + industry, drones, cyber-physical systems — write capability plus export control plus ethics of autonomy.
Health R&D: vaccine manufacturing, diagnostics, genomics, One Health. Regulation (CDSCO, ICMR) and equity of access belong in the same paragraph as the molecule.
Internal security tech: CCTNS flavour, drones on borders, encryption vs lawful access. Always add a rights sentence so GS-III does not become a gadget list.

subjects.title: Environment & Ecology
subjects.overview: Environment is ecology science plus law plus climate politics. Prelims: definitions and conventions. Mains: development vs conservation, and Bihar’s flood–heat–agriculture triangle. Use Shankar selectively; NCERT + current affairs do most of the work.
sources: Down To Earth / The Hindu Environment

modules.title: Core ecology
explain: Ecosystem structure (biotic–abiotic), food chains, ecological pyramids, biomes, nutrient cycles (C, N, P, water). Biodiversity: genetic–species–ecosystem; hotspots (two criteria: endemism + threat); IUCN Red List; CITES; Ramsar wetlands; UNESCO World Heritage natural sites. Know at least one Bihar-relevant wetland/forest issue.

Pollution: air (PM2.5, NCAP), water, plastic, e-waste. Law: EPA 1986, Air/Water Acts, Wildlife Act, Forest Rights Act, EIA process, NGT. Current affairs often turns on EIA exemptions or a court order.

Climate: UNFCCC, Kyoto, Paris, NDCs, mitigation (emissions) vs adaptation (floods, heat, seeds). Bihar is an adaptation geography: floods, heat, changing monsoon, agrarian vulnerability. Disaster management (NDMA, Sendai) overlaps here.

modules.title: India policy, finance and justice
explain: From Stockholm 1972 to EPA 1986 to NGT 2010: institutions matured faster than enforcement. EIA, CRZ, forest clearance, and FRA sit in one clearance-vs-rights diagram. Climate policy: NAPCC missions, NDCs, carbon market pilots, state action plans — Bihar’s SAPCC is adaptation-heavy.
Environment justice: who lives next to the landfill, who loses land to a dam, who breathes brick-kiln air. A GS-III answer that names a community and a remedy scores above a list of Acts.
International: CBDR-RC, climate finance, loss and damage, plastic treaty talks. Link each COP headline back to India’s energy mix and coal districts.

subjects.title: Ethics
subjects.overview: GS-IV rewards clarity, not quotations. Define a value, give a public-service example, then a case. Newspapers in Bihar — floods, exams, welfare targeting — are enough if you stay non-partisan.
sources: Real cases from The Hindu / IE

modules.title: Values, thinkers, cases
explain: Write your own one-line definitions: integrity (honesty when nobody is watching), conflict of interest, compassion, objectivity, non-partisanship, perseverance, empathy, emotional intelligence (reading affect and regulating response). If you cannot apply a thinker (Gandhi’s means–ends, Kautilya’s danda–dharma, Kant’s duty, Aristotle’s golden mean), drop the name.
Case method: facts → stakeholders → options (including do-nothing) → public interest and constitutional values → chosen path and communication. Never write a sermon without an operational step.
Practise on Bihar files: flood relief targeting, teacher/exam integrity, caste data and fairness, police discretion. The interview will probe the same temperament: calm, specific, lawful, kind.
points: Weekly news case: stakeholders → options → public interest.
Bihar administration examples without party colour.

modules.title: Aptitude, attitude and public organisations
explain: Foundational values (2nd ARC): integrity, impartiality, non-partisanship, objectivity, dedication to public service, empathy, tolerance, compassion. Aptitude is the stable pattern; attitude can be trained by leadership, incentives and peer culture.

Emotional intelligence is a field skill: flood camp, angry counter, communal rumour. Name the EI component you used. Work culture and code of ethics vs code of conduct are standard theory — keep them short and then apply.
Probity: RTI, disclosures, social audit, e-procurement, whistle-blower protection, recusal. Corporate ethics and environmental ethics appear when a PSU, contractor or EIA file is in the case.
